chapterTitle: Saved by Mercy, Ready for Every Good Work
themeTitle: “According to His Mercy, He Saved Us”

scripture.text: Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
scripture.understanding: ὑπομίμνῃσκε αὐτούς, “Remind them” — they knew it already; they needed reminding. ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ὑποτάσσεσθαι, “to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities.” Two members of the power family side by side: ἀρχή, rule, the authority of first place, and ἐξουσία, delegated right to act. Both are human government here. πειθαρχεῖν, “to be obedient” — to obey a ruler. πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἑτοίμους εἶναι, “to be ready for every good work” — ἔργον from the work family, ἀγαθός from the good family. Believers are to be the best citizens in town, ready to help whenever good can be done. Crete had a reputation for rebellion; the church was to be different.

scripture.text: to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men.
scripture.understanding: μηδένα βλασφημεῖν, “to speak evil of no one.” A word-family point: ‘speak evil’ here is βλασφημέω, to slander, to damage someone's name — not κακός or πονηρός. ἀμάχους εἶναι, “not to be contentious” — not fighters; ἐπιεικεῖς, “to be gentle” — reasonable, yielding, ready to give way; πᾶσαν ἐνδεικνυμένους πραΰτητα πρὸς πάντας ἀνθρώπους, “showing all humility toward all men.” πραΰτης is meekness — strength under control. ‘All men’ includes rude neighbours and corrupt officials.

scripture.text: For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.
scripture.understanding: Why be gentle with sinful outsiders? ἦμεν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς, “For we were also once” — Paul includes himself. ἀνόητοι, “foolish” — without understanding; ἀπειθεῖς, “disobedient”; πλανώμενοι, “deceived” — wandering off the path; δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις, “serving various lusts and pleasures” — δουλεύω from the servant family: we were slaves, and our masters were desires. ἐν κακίᾳ καὶ φθόνῳ διάγοντες, “living in malice and envy” — κακία from the evil family: malice, ill-will. στυγητοί, “hateful,” μισοῦντες ἀλλήλους, “and hating one another.” This is the ‘before’ picture of every believer.

scripture.text: But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
scripture.understanding: ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία ἐπεφάνη τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν θεοῦ, “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared.” Everything turns on ‘but’. χρηστότης is kindness, goodness that is useful to others. φιλανθρωπία, from the love family, is love for human beings (our ‘philanthropy’): the opposite of the hating and hateful people of verse 3. And ἐπιφαίνω from the appear family again (as in 2:11): God's kindness shone out like the dawn when Christ came.

scripture.text: not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
scripture.understanding: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς, “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves” — ἔργον from the work family. The letter that speaks so much of good works insists they play no part in saving us. ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν αὐτοῦ ἔλεον ἔσωσεν ἡμᾶς, “but according to his mercy, he saved us.” How? διὰ λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας καὶ ἀνακαινώσεως πνεύματος ἁγίου, “through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.” λουτρόν is a bath; παλιγγενεσία, a new genesis, being born again; ἀνακαίνωσις, from the new family, renewal in kind (καινός). Many connect the ‘washing’ with baptism, others with the inner cleansing the Spirit gives; either way, the one who saves is God in His mercy, and the agent of new birth is the Holy Spirit.

scripture.text: whom he poured out on us richly, through Jesus Christ our Savior;
scripture.understanding: οὗ ἐξέχεεν ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς πλουσίως, “whom he poured out on us richly” — ἐκχέω, the very word of Pentecost, when Peter said the exalted Christ had ‘poured out’ the promised Spirit. πλουσίως, abundantly: God did not ration the Spirit. διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, “through Jesus Christ our Savior.” Notice the whole Trinity in verses 4–6: God our Savior (the Father) saved us by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior.

scripture.text: that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
scripture.understanding: ἵνα δικαιωθέντες τῇ ἐκείνου χάριτι, “that being justified by his grace” — δικαιόω, declared righteous: the courtroom verdict, received as a gift. κληρονόμοι γενώμεθα, “we might be made heirs” — those who share an inheritance by lot. κατ᾽ ἐλπίδα ζωῆς αἰωνίου, “according to the hope of eternal life” — ζωή from the life family. The letter began with ‘hope of eternal life’ (1:2), and the gospel summary ends in the same place.

scripture.text: This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you affirm confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men;
scripture.understanding: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, “This saying is faithful” — the last of five ‘faithful sayings’ in the pastoral letters, pointing back to verses 4–7. καὶ περὶ τούτων βούλομαί σε διαβεβαιοῦσθαι, “and concerning these things I desire that you affirm confidently” — insist on them. Why? ἵνα φροντίζωσιν καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι οἱ πεπιστευκότες θεῷ, “so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works.” Salvation is not by works, as verse 5 insisted; but it is always for works. καλός from the good family and ἔργον from the work family. ταῦτά ἐστιν τὰ καλὰ καὶ ὠφέλιμα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, “These things are good and profitable to men.”

scripture.text: but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
scripture.understanding: μωρὰς δὲ ζητήσεις καὶ γενεαλογίας καὶ ἔρεις καὶ μάχας νομικὰς περιΐστασο, “but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law” — περιΐστημι, step around, give a wide berth. These were the false teachers' speciality (1:10, 14). εἰσὶν γὰρ ἀνωφελεῖς καὶ μάταιοι, “for they are unprofitable and vain.” Notice the deliberate contrast: good works are ὠφέλιμα, ‘profitable’ (v. 8); these debates are ἀνωφελεῖς, ‘unprofitable’. Some activity looks spiritual but helps no one.

scripture.text: Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning,
scripture.understanding: αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον, “a factious man” — αἱρετικός (the root of ‘heretic’) here means someone who causes divisions by pushing his own opinions, forming a party. μετὰ μίαν καὶ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν, “after a first and second warning” — νουθεσία, putting sense into the mind: patient admonition, given twice. παραιτοῦ, “Avoid” — decline further dealings. Patience comes first; separation comes last.

scripture.text: knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.
scripture.understanding: εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος, “knowing that such a one is perverted” — ἐκστρέφω, twisted inside out. καὶ ἁμαρτάνει, “and sins” — ἁμαρτάνω, the verb of the sin family's chief word: to miss the mark, and to keep on missing it (present tense). ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος, “being self-condemned” — his refusal of repeated warnings passes sentence on himself. The church does not condemn him; he has condemned himself.

scripture.text: When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there.
scripture.understanding: ὅταν πέμψω Ἀρτεμᾶν πρός σε ἢ Τυχικόν, “When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus” — one of them would replace Titus on Crete. Tychicus later went to Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:12). σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός με εἰς Νικόπολιν, “be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis” — probably Nicopolis in Epirus, on the western coast of Greece. ἐκεῖ γὰρ κέκρικα παραχειμάσαι, “for I have determined to winter there” — sailing stopped in winter. Shortly afterwards Paul writes that Titus had gone to Dalmatia, just north of there (2 Timothy 4:10).

scripture.text: Send Zenas, the lawyer, and Apollos on their journey speedily, that nothing may be lacking for them.
scripture.understanding: Ζηνᾶν τὸν νομικὸν καὶ Ἀπολλῶν σπουδαίως πρόπεμψον, “Send Zenas, the lawyer, and Apollos on their journey speedily.” νομικός, ‘lawyer’, is the same word as the ‘disputes about the law’ in verse 9: not every expert in law is a troublemaker. Apollos was the eloquent teacher from Alexandria (Acts 18:24). προπέμπω means to equip travellers for the road with food, money and companions. ἵνα μηδὲν αὐτοῖς λείπῃ, “that nothing may be lacking for them” — λείπω, the word of 1:5: Titus came to fix what was lacking in the churches; the churches must make sure nothing is lacking for the missionaries.

scripture.text: Let our people also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they may not be unfruitful.
scripture.understanding: μανθανέτωσαν δὲ καὶ οἱ ἡμέτεροι, “Let our people also learn” — learning implies practice and habit. καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι, “to maintain good works” — the phrase of verse 8 again. εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας, “for necessary uses” — real needs, such as helping Zenas and Apollos on their way. ἵνα μὴ ὦσιν ἄκαρποι, “that they may not be unfruitful.” The Cretans' proverb called them ‘idle’ (ἀργός, 1:12); the church is to be fruitful. The last instruction of the letter is about good works.

scripture.text: All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.
scripture.understanding: ἀσπάζονταί σε οἱ μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ πάντες, “All who are with me greet you.” ἄσπασαι τοὺς φιλοῦντας ἡμᾶς ἐν πίστει, “Greet those who love us in faith” — φιλέω from the love family: the warm love of friends, bound together ‘in faith’. The letter that began with the φιλανθρωπία of God (v. 4) ends with the φιλία of believers. ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, “Grace be with you all” — ‘you all’ is plural: the letter was for every believer on Crete. Ἀμήν.

visualMeditations.title: Before and After
visualMeditations.image: Picture two photographs side by side. In the first, a group of people stand in a dark room: their faces are hard, their fists clenched, some turned away from each other, chains hanging from their wrists marked ‘desire’, ‘pleasure’, ‘envy’. In the second, the same people stand in bright sunlight. The chains lie broken on the ground. Their faces are softened; they are smiling, embracing, serving one another. Between the two photographs is a single word written in light: ‘But’.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (v. 3). “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared” (v. 4), “according to his mercy, he saved us” (v. 5). Every believer has a ‘before’ and an ‘after’, and between them is God's mercy. Remembering your own ‘before’ makes you gentle with others who are still in the dark.

visualMeditations.title: The Bath and the River
visualMeditations.image: Picture someone covered in the grime of years, stained deep into the skin, who has tried every soap and scrubbing brush without success. Then they are led to a pool of living water and plunged in. They rise clean — not just on the surface but through and through, as if they had been born again. And as they stand on the bank, a great river begins to pour down from above, not in drops but in torrents, flooding them with life.
visualMeditations.meaning: God “saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly, through Jesus Christ our Savior” (vv. 5–6). Salvation is a bath and a new birth: God cleanses what we could never clean and gives a new beginning we could never create. And the Spirit is not given sparingly but ‘richly’. Ask the Spirit to make you freshly aware of the cleansing and the new life He has given you.

visualMeditations.title: Fruit Trees in a Barren Land
visualMeditations.image: Picture a dry, stony hillside where nothing useful grows. Then picture a farmer planting a grove of fruit trees there, watering them and tending them year after year. In time the trees blossom and bear fruit. Hungry travellers stop to eat; neighbours carry away baskets; the whole valley is fed. The trees did not plant themselves, but now that they are planted, they bear fruit for others.
visualMeditations.meaning: God saved us “not by works” (v. 5), but He saved us so that we would be “careful to maintain good works” (v. 8). The letter's final command is: “Let our people also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they may not be unfruitful” (v. 14). We are trees planted by grace, meant to feed others. Ask the Spirit where the ‘necessary uses’ around you are, and how you can bear fruit for them.

structure.label: Good Citizens and Gentle Neighbours (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Believers must be reminded to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to slander no one, to avoid fighting, and to be gentle and humble toward all people.

structure.label: Saved by God's Mercy (v. 3-7)
structure.body: We too were once foolish, disobedient, deceived and enslaved to desires, living in malice, envy and hatred; but when God our Saviour's kindness and love for humanity appeared, He saved us — not because of our works but by His mercy — through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by grace, we might become heirs of eternal life.

structure.label: Devoted to Good Works, Avoiding Divisions (v. 8-11)
structure.body: This trustworthy saying must be stressed so that believers devote themselves to good works, which are good and profitable; foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law must be avoided as useless, and a divisive person warned twice and then avoided.

structure.label: Final Instructions and Greetings (v. 12-15)
structure.body: Titus is to come to Paul at Nicopolis when Artemas or Tychicus arrives, to help Zenas and Apollos on their journey, and to teach the believers to devote themselves to good works that meet real needs; Paul sends greetings and grace to all.

sections.heading: Gentle Toward All, Because We Were Once Like Them
paragraphs: Chapter 3 turns from life in the church to life in the world. Titus is to “Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men” (vv. 1–2). Believers on an island known for lying and rebellion are to be model citizens: respectful, helpful, peaceable, gentle. Paul taught the same in Romans: “Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1).

Why should Christians be gentle with a corrupt and hostile world? Because “we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another” (v. 3). Paul does not say ‘they are’ but ‘we were’. He describes himself, the former blasphemer and persecutor, as much as anyone. To the Ephesians he wrote, “among whom we also all once lived in the lusts of our flesh” (Ephesians 2:3). Believers have no right to look down on anyone.

Remembering where we came from produces humility, and humility produces gentleness. The word for ‘gentle’ (ἐπιεικής) describes someone who does not insist on their rights; ‘humility’ (πραΰτης) is strength under control. This is not weakness, but the character of Christ. Paul urges the same elsewhere: “Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand” (Philippians 4:5). The gospel changes how we treat those who are still what we once were.

sections.heading: But When the Kindness of God Appeared
paragraphs: Then comes one of the greatest sentences in Scripture: “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit” (vv. 4–5). The ‘but’ is God's intervention. Into a world of hatred came God's φιλανθρωπία, His love for human beings, shining out in Christ. Paul wrote similarly to the Ephesians: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us” (Ephesians 2:4).

Salvation is entirely God's work. It is ‘not by works’ — not our religious efforts, not our moral record. It is ‘according to his mercy’. And it is a total transformation: a washing that cleanses and a new birth that begins a new life, worked by the Holy Spirit. Jesus told Nicodemus, “unless one is born of water and spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom” (John 3:5). Paul reminded the Corinthians, “but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

God “poured out on us richly” this Spirit “through Jesus Christ our Savior” (v. 6), “that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (v. 7). The Father, the Son and the Spirit work together in our salvation. We are justified — declared righteous by grace — and made heirs. Paul says in Romans, “and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The beggar becomes a son with an inheritance.

sections.heading: Careful to Maintain Good Works
paragraphs: Immediately after this glorious statement of grace, Paul says: “This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you affirm confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works” (v. 8). Grace is not the enemy of good works; it is their source. We are saved not by works but for works. Paul says it plainly to the Ephesians: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

In contrast, Titus must avoid what is useless: “but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain” (v. 9). Good works are profitable; these debates profit no one. And a divisive person, after two warnings, must be avoided, because “such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (v. 11). The church must protect its unity and its time for what really matters.

The letter ends with travel plans and greetings, but even here good works appear. Titus is to help Zenas and Apollos on their journey “that nothing may be lacking for them” (v. 13). And the last instruction is, “Let our people also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they may not be unfruitful” (v. 14). Jesus said, “In this is my Father glorified, that you bear much fruit” (John 15:8). The church on Crete, among people called idle, was to be known for fruitful, practical love.

ntConnection.heading: Mercy, New Birth and the Spirit Poured Out
paragraphs: Titus 3:4–7 is a summary of the gospel that echoes across the New Testament. Paul wrote to the Ephesians, “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8), “not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:9). Believers are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24). And “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Spirit poured out richly fulfils the promise quoted by Peter at Pentecost: “It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:17). Peter explained that the risen Christ, “having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this, which you now see and hear” (Acts 2:33). Paul says the same of God's love: “God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5).

The instruction to be subject to authorities and gentle toward all fits the wider apostolic teaching. Peter writes, “Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake” (1 Peter 2:13). Paul urges, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). And he warns the Romans to “look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and turn away from them” (Romans 16:17), much as Titus is told to deal with the factious man.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “fondness of mankind, i.e. benevolence ("philanthropy").” In Greek culture it was praised in kings who were generous to their subjects. Luke uses it of the islanders of Malta who welcomed shipwrecked Paul. Here it is God's own love for humanity, appearing in Christ. Set against the hateful, hating people of verse 3, it shows that God loved people who did not love Him or one another.

Strong's: “(spiritual) rebirth (the state or the act), i.e. (figuratively) spiritual renovation; specially, Messianic restoration.” It combines πάλιν, again, and γένεσις, birth or beginning. Jesus used it of the renewal of all things at His return (Matthew 19:28). Paul uses it of the new birth of the believer. What God will one day do for the whole creation, He has already begun in everyone who is in Christ.

Strong's: “renovation.” It is built from ἀνά, again, and καινός, new in quality, the first member of the ‘new’ word family. Paul uses it in Romans 12:2 for the renewing of the mind. Regeneration is the new beginning; renewal is the ongoing work of the Spirit making us new in kind. Both come from God's mercy, not our effort.

Strong's: “to pour forth; figuratively, to bestow.” It is used of blood poured out, of wine spilled and of God's Spirit poured out at Pentecost. Paul adds πλουσίως, ‘richly’. God does not ration His Spirit or give Him reluctantly. The same generous God who saved us by mercy pours His Spirit on us abundantly, through Jesus Christ.

Strong's: “barren (literally or figuratively).” It is used of seed choked by thorns in the parable of the sower, and of the ‘unfruitful deeds of darkness’ in Ephesians. Paul's final instruction to Titus is that believers learn good works so they are not barren. A life saved by grace is meant to bear fruit that meets real needs: food for the hungry, help for travellers, kindness for neighbours.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: As this letter closes, the Holy Spirit speaks to you about remembering your ‘before’, rejoicing in God's mercy, and bearing fruit.

items.title: Remember What You Were
items.body: The Spirit reminds you that you too were once foolish, deceived and enslaved. This is not to shame you, but to make you gentle with others who are still where you were. Ask Him to replace any harshness or superiority toward unbelievers with the humility and kindness of someone who has been rescued.

items.title: Rest in His Mercy
items.body: You were saved not by works of righteousness you did, but by His mercy. The Spirit wants to free you from trying to earn God's love. Let Him wash away any lingering sense that you must prove yourself to God. You have been washed, reborn, renewed, justified and made an heir. Receive it with gratitude.

items.title: Bear Fruit for Real Needs
items.body: The Spirit has been poured out richly on you so that you may bear fruit. He wants your life to be practical and useful to others. Ask Him to show you the ‘necessary uses’ around you this week — people with real needs He wants you to meet.

audit.title: The Citizenship Check
audit.body: How do you speak about leaders and authorities, and about people you disagree with? Do your words ‘speak evil of no one’ (v. 2)? Identify one habit of speech to change.

audit.title: The Before-and-After Check
audit.body: Write down two or three things that described your life before Christ (v. 3), and what God has changed by His mercy (vv. 4–7). Thank Him for each change.

audit.title: The Profitable Check
audit.body: List how you spent your spiritual energy this past week. Mark what was ‘profitable’ (good works, v. 8) and what was ‘unprofitable’ (empty arguments, v. 9). Choose to shift one hour from the second to the first.

practices.title: Memorise the Gospel of Titus 3:4–7
practices.body: Commit Titus 3:4–7 to memory over the next two weeks. Say it every morning as a reminder that you are saved by mercy, washed, renewed, justified and made an heir. When you feel condemned or proud, recite it again. Share it with someone who is struggling to believe God could accept them.

practices.title: Meet a Necessary Need
practices.body: This month, look for a real, practical need in your church or community — a missionary or traveller who needs support, a family facing hardship, a neighbour who needs help. Meet it generously, as Titus was to equip Zenas and Apollos ‘that nothing may be lacking for them’ (v. 13). Invite others to join you, so that ‘our people also learn to maintain good works’.

prayerReflection: “Father, I remember that I too was once foolish, disobedient and deceived, enslaved to my desires, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating others. But when Your kindness and Your love for humanity appeared in Jesus Christ, You saved me — not because of works of righteousness I had done, but because of Your mercy. Thank You for the washing of new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom You poured out on me richly through Jesus Christ my Saviour. Thank You that I am justified by Your grace and made an heir of eternal life. Let this truth make me gentle and humble toward everyone, respectful to those in authority, slow to speak evil of anyone, and ready for every good work. Keep me from foolish arguments and divisions. Teach me to devote myself to good works that meet real needs, so that my life is not unfruitful. Grace be with me and with all Your people. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Saul the Persecutor Becomes Paul the Apostle
storyConnections.summary: Saul was ‘breathing threats and slaughter’ against the disciples, travelling to Damascus to arrest believers. He was the very picture of Titus 3:3: deceived, disobedient, filled with hatred. Then “suddenly a light from the sky shone around him” (Acts 9:3), and he heard Jesus' voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Blinded, he was led into the city. Three days later Ananias laid hands on him, and “something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized” (Acts 9:18). Paul later wrote that he had been “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). When he wrote ‘we were also once…’ in Titus 3:3, he was describing himself.

storyConnections.title: Apollos Sent on His Way
storyConnections.summary: Apollos was “a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man” (Acts 18:24) who knew the Scriptures well. After Priscilla and Aquila taught him more accurately, he wanted to go to Achaia, and the believers in Ephesus encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. In Corinth he greatly helped those who had believed. Paul later wrote, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). In Titus 3:13, Apollos is travelling again, and the church on Crete is to supply him generously so that nothing is lacking. Supporting gospel workers on their journeys is one of the ‘good works for necessary uses’.

storyConnections.title: The Kindness of the Islanders of Malta
storyConnections.summary: After Paul's ship was wrecked on the voyage to Rome — having sailed past Crete — the survivors struggled ashore on Malta, cold and soaked. Luke records that “The natives showed us uncommon kindness” (Acts 28:2) — the word is φιλανθρωπία — building a fire and welcoming them all. Paul then healed the father of Publius, the chief man of the island, and many others. When they left, “they put on board the things that we needed” (Acts 28:10). The story shows kindness meeting real needs, and gospel power flowing through a prisoner. It is a small picture of God's own φιλανθρωπία, which ‘appeared’ in Christ, and of the practical good works Titus 3 calls for.
